meta.title: U.S. Renewable Energy Policy — Current Status

policies.policy_title: Technology-neutral clean-electricity credits under IRC sections 45Y and 48E
policies.short_summary: Sections 45Y and 48E provide technology-neutral production and investment credits under final regulations effective January 15, 2025. Public Law 119-21 later added a wind-and-solar termination rule and prohibited-foreign-entity eligibility restrictions addressed in Notices 2025-42 and 2026-15.
policies.status_explanation: The statutory credits and T.D. 10024 final regulations are in force. For applicable wind and solar facilities, the post-2027 termination applies when construction begins after July 4, 2026; Notice 2025-42 supplies the beginning-of-construction rules. Public Law 119-21 also added prohibited-foreign-entity restrictions, for which Notice 2026-15 provides interim safe harbors and reliance rules pending proposed regulations.
policies.effective_requirements: Apply the statutory and final-regulation eligibility rules, including a greenhouse-gas emissions rate not greater than zero; for applicable wind or solar facilities, apply Notice 2025-42 to the statutory termination timing; and for facilities or energy storage technology within the applicable construction window, evaluate prohibited-foreign-entity status and material-assistance restrictions using Public Law 119-21 and Notice 2026-15 reliance rules.
policies.inactive_or_limited_scope: The special wind-and-solar termination is limited to applicable facilities as defined by Public Law 119-21; it does not itself establish that every other 45Y or 48E technology is unavailable.
policies.next_milestone: December 31, 2027 placed-in-service boundary for applicable wind and solar facilities; forthcoming proposed prohibited-foreign-entity regulations are also material.

policies.policy_title: Domestic-content bonus-credit requirements for clean-energy credits
policies.short_summary: The domestic-content bonus is available when statutory steel, iron, and manufactured-product requirements are met; IRS Notice 2025-08 provides an updated elective safe harbor and certification and recordkeeping directions.
policies.status_explanation: The IRA statutory bonus remains available subject to its requirements. Notice 2025-08 provides reliance rules and an elective safe harbor; it does not replace the statutory domestic-content test.
policies.effective_requirements: A taxpayer must satisfy the domestic-content requirement, attach the Domestic Content Certification Statement to the applicable return, and retain substantiating records; taxpayers relying on the updated elective safe harbor must make the affirmative election and apply one safe harbor consistently.
policies.inactive_or_limited_scope: The notice's reliance windows and elective safe harbors are limited by their stated beginning-of-construction and future-modification conditions; no conclusion is made here about qualification of a particular component or project.
policies.next_milestone: Any future IRS modification, update, or withdrawal of the First Updated Elective Safe Harbor affects its stated reliance window.

policies.short_summary: Energy-community bonus amounts or rates apply when statutory location requirements are met; Notice 2026-39 is the current annual statistical-area and coal-closure update, applicable for listed statistical areas from June 9, 2026 and adding coal-closure and correction tracts.
policies.status_explanation: The statutory energy-community provisions remain in force. Notice 2026-39 supplies the current Statistical Area and new Coal Closure information, while preserving the cumulative use of specified earlier coal-closure appendices. The annual notice does not address Brownfield-category determinations.
policies.effective_requirements: Determine whether the project meets the applicable statutory energy-community category. For current Statistical Area status, use Notice 2026-39 from June 9, 2026 until the next annual list. For Coal Closure status, combine the current notice's appendices with the earlier appendices it identifies, including retroactive correction treatment stated for Appendix 3.
policies.inactive_or_limited_scope: Notice 2026-39 does not provide Brownfield Category information and its appendices are not applicable to the section 48C qualifying advanced energy project credit.
affected_entities: communities near fossil-energy employment or coal closures
policies.next_milestone: The next IRS annual energy-community notice based on 2026 unemployment rates, expected in 2027; project-specific location and timing review remains necessary.

policies.policy_title: 2025 four-country crystalline-silicon photovoltaic AD/CVD order set
policies.policy_area: Solar trade remedies and project supply
policies.short_summary: Commerce issued AD/CVD orders on crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells and covered modules from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam after affirmative Commerce and USITC determinations; the July 2025 correction controls specified Vietnam scope and Malaysia exclusion corrections.
policies.status_explanation: The June 2025 AD orders were corrected in the July 2025 Federal Register notice. The record identifies scope and producer/exporter limitations rather than assigning a single duty rate to all imports.
policies.effective_requirements: For covered crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells and modules from the four named countries, apply the written scope of the AD/CVD orders, including the July 2025 correction; importers must evaluate country, product scope, and applicable producer/exporter treatment.
policies.inactive_or_limited_scope: The orders exclude specified products and the correction states that the Hanwha Q Cells Malaysia producer/exporter combination is excluded from the Malaysia AD order; the written scope is dispositive over HTSUS headings supplied for convenience.
lead_agencies: Department of Commerce, International Trade Administration
policies.next_milestone: Monitor Commerce scope rulings, administrative reviews, and Customs implementation for covered imports.

policies.short_summary: Order No. 2023 revises FERC's pro forma generator-interconnection procedures and agreements through a first-ready, first-served cluster-study process, readiness requirements, study deadlines and penalties, and technology-related reforms.
policies.status_explanation: Order No. 2023 became effective on 2023-11-06 and remains in force as modified by the October 25, 2023 limited rehearing order, Order No. 2023-A, and the August 20, 2024 errata notice. FERC stated in June 2026 that rulewide compliance was not fully complete. The D.C. Circuit heard Advanced Energy United v. FERC on 2025-09-26, and a FERC brief filed 2026-05-20 states that the challenges remained pending; official searches through 2026-07-26 located no later controlling disposition.
policies.effective_requirements: Public-utility transmission providers must revise their interconnection procedures and agreements to comply with the Order No. 2023 legal chain, subject to Commission-approved compliance filings and permitted variations.
policies.inactive_or_limited_scope: The rule does not itself establish one tariff-effective date for every transmission provider. Provider-specific compliance outcomes are not treated here as order-wide completion findings.
policies.next_milestone: Continue provider-specific compliance proceedings and monitor D.C. Circuit No. 23-1282, et al., for disposition.

policies.policy_title: FERC Order No. 1920 long-term regional transmission planning and cost allocation
policies.short_summary: Order No. 1920 requires long-term regional transmission planning and ex ante cost-allocation processes; Orders No. 1920-A and 1920-B modify and clarify the rule, including state participation and cost-allocation provisions.
policies.status_explanation: Order No. 1920 became effective on 2024-08-12, and Order No. 1920-A's changes became effective on 2025-01-06 as confirmed by Order No. 1920-B. FERC's order-wide compliance schedule lists two regional filings and deadlines extending into 2027. FERC's current case page and 2026-01-05 respondent brief document consolidated Fourth Circuit review in Appalachian Voices v. FERC, Nos. 24-1650, et al.; official searches through 2026-07-26 located no later controlling disposition.
policies.effective_requirements: Transmission providers must conduct long-term regional planning using at least three long-term scenarios over a 20-year-or-longer horizon, establish ex ante cost-allocation method(s), engage relevant state entities, and make the required regional compliance filings.
policies.inactive_or_limited_scope: Compliance schedules and tariff outcomes differ by transmission-planning region. This record does not treat any one region's filing, extension, or Commission action as nationwide completion or acceptance.
policies.next_milestone: Regional first and interregional compliance-filing deadlines continue through 2026-2027; monitor Appalachian Voices v. FERC, Nos. 24-1650, et al. (4th Cir.).

policies.policy_title: CEQ NEPA-regulation rescission and agency-specific implementation transition
policies.short_summary: CEQ's government-wide NEPA implementing regulations at 40 CFR parts 1500-1508 were removed; agencies continue to implement the NEPA statute through their own procedures, which are being revised or have been revised.
policies.status_explanation: CEQ's final rule, effective January 8, 2026, adopted the rescission without change. CEQ's September 2025 guidance directs a continuing agency-specific transition, and DOI finalized its own updated procedures on February 24, 2026. No litigation directly challenging the CEQ rescission was identified; Seven County is interpretive NEPA precedent, not rescission litigation.
policies.effective_requirements: Federal agencies must implement NEPA's statutory environmental-review requirements and develop methods and procedures in consultation with CEQ. | CEQ's former 40 CFR parts 1500-1508 are removed from the CFR. | DOI applies its revised 43 CFR part 46 provisions and DOI NEPA Handbook to DOI processes.
policies.inactive_or_limited_scope: The rescission does not repeal or amend the NEPA statute. | DOI's 2026 rule is agency-specific and does not itself set procedures for other agencies. | Seven County concerns review of an STB railway approval; it is controlling precedent on NEPA judicial review, not a project approval for renewable energy.
affected_entities: Renewable-energy project sponsors needing federal approvals
States, Tribes, and public participants in federal reviews
policies.next_milestone: Agency-specific procedure revisions and any later court challenge or legislative change; no single CEQ replacement regulation is identified in the reviewed sources.

policies.policy_title: Federal offshore-wind policy: operative OCS leasing withdrawal and vacated permitting pause
policies.short_summary: The January 20, 2025 Presidential Memorandum has a mixed current effect: Section 1's OCS wind-leasing withdrawal remains operative, while the agency-wide permitting pause implementing Section 2(a) was declared unlawful and vacated on December 8, 2025; the First Circuit entered judgment dismissing the government's voluntary appeal on June 15, 2026.
policies.status_explanation: Section 1 states that the OCS leasing withdrawal remains until revoked and was expressly outside New York v. Trump. The District of Massachusetts vacated the agencies' Section 2(a) Wind Order on December 8, 2025. On June 15, 2026, the First Circuit entered judgment voluntarily dismissing appeal No. 26-1174 and ordered the mandate to issue forthwith, leaving the district judgment undisturbed. The `delayed` implementation value reflects continuing unavailability of new OCS leasing under Section 1, not continued implementation of the vacated Section 2(a) pause.
policies.effective_requirements: Section 1 continues to withdraw all OCS areas from disposition for new or renewed wind-energy leasing until the memorandum is revoked. | Existing lease rights remain unaffected by Section 1's text, subject to separate lawful project- or lease-specific actions.
policies.inactive_or_limited_scope: The agency-wide Wind Order implementing Section 2(a)'s permitting pause was declared unlawful and vacated; it is not treated as an active approval moratorium. | Section 1 was not at issue in New York v. Trump and remains separate from the vacated Section 2(a) implementation. | Later BOEM project suspensions and injunctions are project-specific and do not change the government-wide Section 1/Section 2(a) split.
affected_entities: Offshore-wind project developers seeking federal approvals
State and Tribal governments participating in reviews
policies.next_milestone: Revocation or modification of the Section 1 leasing withdrawal, completion or publication of the federal review, or a new lawful leasing or permitting action; New York v. Trump is closed after appeal dismissal.

Order No. 2023 establishes the order-wide interconnection reforms.
The October 25, 2023 order sets Order No. 2023 aside in part to extend compliance-filing deadlines.
Order No. 2023-A modifies and clarifies the final rule.
The August 20, 2024 errata notice makes additional revisions to the pro forma LGIP, LGIA, and SGIA.
The June 2026 FERC statement reports that the rulewide compliance process remains incomplete.
The D.C. Circuit oral-argument record documents judicial review of Order No. 2023.
FERC's May 2026 brief reports that the Order No. 2023 challenges remained pending after argument.
Order No. 1920 establishes long-term regional planning and cost-allocation reforms.
Order No. 1920-A modifies and clarifies the final rule on rehearing.
Order No. 1920-B further addresses rehearing of and clarifies Order No. 1920-A.
FERC's schedule describes the two order-wide compliance filings and regional extensions.
FERC's current case page records consolidated Fourth Circuit challenges to the Order No. 1920 legal chain.
FERC's respondent brief addresses the consolidated petitions for review of Orders No. 1920, 1920-A, and 1920-B.
Executive Order directs the CEQ actions and agency-procedure coordination comprising this policy transition.
Final CEQ rule removes the former government-wide CEQ regulations.
DOI finalizes DOI-only procedures following the CEQ rescission.
Supreme Court decision supplies binding NEPA judicial-review precedent but does not decide the CEQ rescission.
Current CEQ guidance explains the nonbinding, agency-specific implementation transition after rescission.
Presidential Memorandum establishes the still-operative Section 1 OCS leasing withdrawal and originally directed the now-vacated Section 2(a) Wind Order.
BOEM records one project-process action implementing the broader memorandum.
DOJ historically reported New York v. Trump as pending; later controlling sources supersede that status.
The district court vacates the agencies' Section 2(a) Wind Order while expressly excluding Section 1 from the litigation.
The First Circuit judgment dismisses the appeal and leaves the district-court Section 2(a) vacatur undisturbed.

assessments.assessment_summary: CEQ's final rule effective January 8, 2026 removes 40 CFR parts 1500-1508; NEPA's statutory requirements remain in force.
assessments.analyst_inference: The final rule directly controls the status of CEQ's regulations; the retained statutory duties are stated in the rule and are not inferred to have been repealed.

assessments.assessment_summary: Current CEQ guidance establishes a continuing agency-specific transition; DOI has completed its revised rule and handbook approach, while agencies with ongoing revisions continue using existing procedures adjusted for current law and guidance.
assessments.analyst_inference: The current CEQ guidance expressly describes ongoing agency revisions, while DOI's completed rule demonstrates that implementation timing is non-uniform across agencies.

assessments.assessment_summary: No litigation directly challenging the CEQ rescission was identified in the reviewed official sources; Seven County is retained only as interpretive NEPA context.
assessments.analyst_inference: `none_identified` is a bounded search result, not proof that no case exists. Seven County is not treated as litigation deciding the rescission and its link is noncontrolling.

assessments.assessment_summary: Section 1's OCS leasing withdrawal remains operative and was outside the case, while the agencies' Section 2(a) Wind Order was vacated.
assessments.analyst_inference: The cluster is intentionally mixed: no reviewed official source records revocation of Section 1, and the district order expressly says Section 1 was not at issue before vacating the Section 2(a) agency Wind Order.

assessments.assessment_summary: New OCS wind leasing remains unavailable under Section 1, but agencies may not continue the vacated Section 2(a) blanket permitting pause; project approvals and suspensions proceed under their own authorities and records.
assessments.analyst_inference: The allowed value `delayed` is used for the continuing leasing constraint only. It does not state or imply that the vacated Section 2(a) Wind Order remains in implementation.

assessments.assessment_summary: The district court vacated the Section 2(a) agency Wind Order, and on June 15, 2026 the First Circuit entered judgment voluntarily dismissing the federal defendants-appellants' appeal.
assessments.citation_locator: No. 26-1174, Document 00118461865, Judgment and docket header; ECF No. 234, pp. 1-4, 47
assessments.analyst_inference: `decided` denotes the terminal procedural disposition of this appeal, not a First Circuit merits affirmance. The dismissal left the district judgment undisturbed and concerns the Section 2(a) Wind Order, not Section 1 or later project-specific actions.
